question: In methanol poisoning, an elevated osmolar gap is most useful early (before metabolism), while a high anion gap metabolic acidosis with normal osmolar gap indicates late-stage poisoning where the methanol has already been converted to formic acid.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is TRUE. The osmolar gap reflects the parent alcohol (early), while the anion gap reflects formic acid accumulation (late). Understanding this temporal relationship is critical — a late presenter with visual loss may have a deceptively normal osmolar gap but catastrophic anion gap acidosis from formate.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Exactly right. Early methanol poisoning: high osmolar gap (unmeasured alcohol molecules), normal/near-normal anion gap. Late methanol poisoning: methanol metabolised to formic acid → osmolar gap normalises, but HIGH ANION GAP acidosis develops. The worst clinical scenario is a patient presenting late with visual symptoms + severe HAGMA + near-normal osmolar gap — this indicates maximal metabolite accumulation.
